meta.name: Irish Setter Grooming Guide
meta.excerpt: The Irish Setter's mahogany feathered coat is lower maintenance than it looks — weekly brushing of the feathering areas and regular ear cleaning covers most of it. No professional grooming required.
meta.meta_description: Irish Setter grooming guide: weekly brushing routine for the feathered coat, ear cleaning protocol for long drop ears, bathing schedule, and feathering trim...

hero.alt: Irish Setter being groomed, showing the rich mahogany long silky coat with flowing feathering texture

intro.label: The Irish Setter Coat
intro.heading: A Silky Single Coat With Deceptively Simple Care
intro.html:
Irish Setters carry one of the most photographed coats in the entire Sporting Group — long, glossy, and a deep mahogany-to-chestnut red — but the actual weekly workload is lighter than the coat's dramatic look suggests. The body itself is covered in short, flat, glossy hair with a single layer and essentially no dense undercoat underneath. All of the length and drama sits in the feathering: the ears, the backs of the front legs, the chest, the belly, and the tail. That's where nearly every grooming minute goes. Because there's no woolly undercoat pushing hair out twice a year, an Irish Setter doesn't "blow coat" the way a Sheltie or a Husky does. Shedding is a slow, steady trickle year-round rather than a seasonal flood, and the rich red color hides loose hair on furniture and dark upholstery far better than a paler coat would.

That doesn't mean the coat is maintenance-free. Length and fine texture come with their own cost — the feathering snags burrs, foxtails, mud, and twigs on every field outing, and it will mat behind the ears and in the soft skin under the front legs within a week or two if it isn't brushed through regularly. This is, after all, a bird dog built to work dense cover, and a 90-to-120-minute daily exercise routine in fields, woods, or water means the coat is almost always in motion. Grooming an Irish Setter well is less about a rigid calendar and more about damage control after every hike, swim, or romp through tall grass.

From Puppy Coat to Adult Feathering

Irish Setter puppies are born with a short, soft, nearly solid-colored coat and none of the signature feathering. That feathering begins coming in gradually between roughly 6 and 12 months and typically isn't fully mature until somewhere between 18 months and 2 years — a timeline that tracks with how slowly this breed matures overall, since many Irish Setters are still behaviorally puppyish well into their third or fourth year. Ironically, the transitional adolescent coat needs more brushing than either the puppy coat or the settled adult coat: the incoming feathering is finer, silkier, and more prone to tangling before it thickens into its mature texture, and small mats behind the ears or along the tail can form before an owner even registers that the texture has changed. Establishing the weekly brushing habit early, while there's little coat to actually work through, means the dog is already comfortable with the process by the time the feathering shows up in earnest.

The Grooming Toolkit

A modest kit covers essentially everything this breed needs for home maintenance:

  • Pin brush ($12–$20) — the primary tool for the feathering; the flexible pins glide through length without pulling.
  • Wide-tooth steel comb ($8–$15) — run through each feathered area after brushing to catch anything the pin brush missed.
  • Slicker brush ($10–$18, optional) — useful for a final smoothing pass on the body coat, used lightly since there's no undercoat to pull.
  • Detangling spray ($8–$15) — a quick spritz on the feathering before brushing after a muddy or dusty outing makes the difference between a five-minute session and a fight.
  • Veterinary ear cleaning solution and cotton balls ($10–$15 per bottle) — non-negotiable given how much this breed's ear shape works against it.
  • Dog shampoo and conditioner formulated for long or silky coats ($12–$25) — conditioner on the feathering after every bath meaningfully cuts down on future tangling.

care.label: Weekly Care
care.heading: The Working Routine: Brushing, Ears, Bathing, and the Rest
care.html:
Brushing the Feathering, Not the Whole Dog

The good news for owners of a 60–70 lb dog is that you're not brushing all of that surface area every session — the body coat mostly takes care of itself. Spend your weekly session on the areas that actually tangle: behind the ears, down the chest, under the belly, along the backs of the legs, and the tail. Work the pin brush through each section in layers rather than skimming the surface, then follow with the wide-tooth comb to confirm nothing's left knotted underneath. A thorough pass takes 15–20 minutes on a settled adult coat, longer during the adolescent coat-change period or after a day spent working cover. Dogs that get their full 90–120 minutes of daily exercise in fields, woods, or water need this checked more often than the calendar alone would suggest — the coat picks up debris faster than it picks up dirt.

Ears Come First With This Breed

If there's one grooming task that matters more for an Irish Setter than for most other breeds, it's ear care. The long, heavy drop ears sit close to the head and block airflow into the canal, trapping moisture and wax and creating exactly the warm, damp environment that ear infections thrive in. Chronic otitis is one of the more common vet visits for this breed, and it's largely preventable with routine cleaning rather than something to address only after symptoms appear. Wipe the outer ear canal with a veterinary cleaning solution and cotton balls every one to two weeks — more often for dogs that swim regularly, since this is a breed that will happily spend an afternoon in a pond given the chance. Watch for head shaking, scratching at the ears, a sour or yeasty smell, or any discharge; those signs call for a veterinary visit rather than more frequent home cleaning, since by that point an infection is usually already established.

Bath Frequency and the Feathering Trim

A bath every 6–8 weeks, or after something genuinely dirty, keeps the coat and skin in good shape without stripping the natural oils that give the coat its shine. Use lukewarm water and a shampoo made for silky or long coats, work conditioner specifically into the feathering, and rinse thoroughly — leftover product residue is a common cause of dull-looking coat and mild skin irritation. Towel-dry first, then finish with a low-heat dryer while brushing the feathering in the direction it grows; air-drying alone tends to leave the feathering slightly wavy rather than sleek. Some owners trim the feathering back a bit, particularly around the feet and the back of the hocks, purely to cut down on what tracks in from outside — this is entirely cosmetic and can be done at home with a pair of blunt-tipped shears or left to a groomer on an as-needed basis rather than a fixed schedule.

Nails, Teeth, and Paws

Nails need trimming roughly every 2–4 weeks; if you can hear them clicking on hardwood, they're overdue. A guillotine clipper or a grinder both work well — the grinder tends to be less stressful for dogs who dislike the pinch of a clipper, and it's easier to stop before hitting the quick. Brush teeth two to three times a week with an enzymatic dog toothpaste; large sporting breeds are not immune to periodontal disease, and it's cheaper to prevent than to treat. After every outing through brush or tall grass, run a hand down each leg and check between the toes for embedded seeds or burrs — this breed's feathering on the feet hides debris well, and a lodged grass awn can work its way into the skin within a day or two if missed.

special.label: Managing the Field Dog Coat
special.heading: Field Work, Seasons, Costs, and the Mistakes That Cause Problems
special.html:
An Irish Setter that gets the exercise this breed actually needs — hiking, running, swimming, working dense cover — is going to bring some of that outdoors home in the coat every single time. Check the feathering immediately after any outing through brush, tall grass, or water, before debris has a chance to work its way in and felt into a mat. A quick once-over with fingers, followed by a real brushing session if anything's tangled, takes a few minutes and prevents the kind of matting that otherwise requires cutting the hair out rather than combing it out.

Building Tolerance From Puppyhood

Start handling ears, paws, mouth, and tail daily from the day the puppy comes home, well before there's any feathering to actually brush. The coat that requires weekly attention as an adult doesn't exist yet at eight weeks, but the calm acceptance of being handled all over is exactly what makes grooming manageable once that coat arrives. An Irish Setter that's used to having its ears touched, its feet held, and its mouth opened for a few seconds every day rarely turns grooming or vet visits into a wrestling match later on — and given how slowly this breed matures, that patience-building period lasts longer than it does for most dogs.

Where This Coat Sits Among Grooming Types

Coat type is what decides brushing frequency, tool choice, and whether a professional groomer is ever strictly necessary. Broadly:

  • Smooth or short single coats shed a steady, low-level amount year-round and rarely need more than a rubber curry brush.
  • Dense double coats carry a soft undercoat beneath a longer guard-hair layer and shed heavily in concentrated multi-week bursts each spring and fall.
  • Wiry, broken coats need hand-stripping or clipping to maintain their texture and color.
  • The Irish Setter's silky single coat with feathering falls into none of those categories cleanly — it sheds steadily like a smooth coat, but the length in the feathering behaves more like a long-haired breed and needs the tangle-prevention routine of one, without ever producing the seasonal "blowout" volume a true double coat does.

A Realistic Seasonal Calendar

Because there's no heavy undercoat to shed in bulk, an Irish Setter's coat care doesn't swing wildly by season the way it does for double-coated breeds. What does change: shorter, cooler days in fall and winter mean more time outdoors in wet leaves and mud, which pushes bath frequency toward the 6-week end of the range and makes post-walk feathering checks non-negotiable. Late spring through summer brings foxtails, seed heads, and burrs in earnest in most parts of the country, along with far more swimming — both of which mean more frequent ear cleaning and closer attention to the feathering on the legs and tail. Shedding itself stays fairly level across the year, with a very mild uptick in spring as the coat lightens slightly for warmer weather.

Professional Grooming: What It Costs and How Often

Most Irish Setter owners can handle this coat entirely at home, which sets it apart from double-coated and curly-coated breeds that require a fixed professional schedule.

ServiceTypical CostFrequency
Bath and blow-dry only$35–$60Every 6–8 weeks, optional — most owners do this at home
Full groom with feathering trim and tidy-up$55–$85Every 8–12 weeks if used at all
Nail trim and ear clean add-on visit$15–$25Between full grooms if you'd rather not do it at home

Because this breed doesn't require clipping or de-shedding tools to stay healthy, there's no equivalent of the every-4-week full groom that curly-coated breeds need. A starter home kit (pin brush, comb, ear cleaner, shampoo, and conditioner) runs roughly $70–$120 and lasts well over a year, which makes home care the far cheaper long-term option for most owners; a professional visit is really about convenience or a tidier finish rather than necessity.

Common Mistakes Owners Make With This Coat

  • Skipping the post-swim ear routine. Water trapped behind the ear flap after a lake swim is one of the most common triggers for infection in this breed specifically — dry the ears with a drying solution or a soft towel every time your Irish Setter goes in the water.
  • Brushing only the surface of the feathering. A quick pass over the top leaves the base of the feathering, closest to the skin, untouched — that's exactly where mats start behind the ears and under the legs.
  • Bathing too often "to keep the red coat shiny." More than monthly bathing dries out the skin and dulls the coat rather than brightening it; the shine comes from a healthy skin barrier and regular brushing, not frequent shampooing.
  • Ignoring embedded grass seeds because the feathering hides them. A foxtail that migrates under the skin can cause a painful abscess or, in the ears and nose, a serious veterinary emergency — check the feet and legs after every outing in grass country.
  • Waiting until shedding season to start brushing during the adolescent coat change. Owners who brush weekly through the puppy stage and then relax once the feathering starts coming in often get caught off guard by tangling right at the point the coat needs the most attention.

More Grooming Questions Answered

My Irish Setter's feathering gets soaked and muddy on every walk — what's realistic?

Toweling off the legs, chest, and tail immediately after a muddy walk, then doing a proper brush-through once the coat is fully dry, is more effective than trying to brush wet, muddy feathering. Wet hair mats far more easily under a brush, so let it dry first unless you're rinsing mud out in the tub.

Does the Irish Setter's coat need a summer trim to stay cool?

No — this is a single coat without heavy insulating undercoat, so there's little benefit to shaving it down for summer, and doing so exposes red-coated skin to sunburn. A light trim of the feathering for cleanliness is fine; a full shave-down isn't necessary for temperature regulation the way it might be discussed for a double-coated breed.

Is it normal for an adolescent Irish Setter to mat more than a puppy or adult?

Yes. The coat transitioning in between roughly 6 months and 2 years is finer and tangles more easily than either the puppy coat or the eventual mature feathering, so this is exactly the stretch where brushing frequency should go up rather than down.

faq.q: Does an Irish Setter need regular trips to a professional groomer?
faq.a: Not as a requirement. This breed's silky single coat with feathering is manageable at home with a weekly brush-through of the ears, chest, legs, and tail, plus a bath every 6–8 weeks. Some owners do book an occasional professional visit for a tidier feathering trim or a thorough blow-dry, but unlike double-coated or curly-coated breeds, there's no fixed 4-to-8-week grooming schedule this breed actually requires.

faq.q: How often do I really need to clean my Irish Setter's ears?
faq.a: Every 1–2 weeks at minimum, and more often for dogs that swim regularly. The heavy, low-set drop ears trap warmth and moisture against the canal, which is exactly the environment chronic ear infections need to take hold, and this breed is genuinely prone to them. If infections keep recurring despite consistent cleaning, ask your vet whether the ear canal itself needs a closer look rather than assuming more cleaning will fix it.

faq.q: Why does my Irish Setter's coat mat behind the ears and under the legs specifically?
faq.a: Those are the feathering areas — the only parts of this otherwise short, flat coat that grow long enough to tangle. Friction from collars and harnesses, plus the warm, slightly damp skin under the ear flap and armpit, makes those two spots mat first and fastest. A weekly brush-through focused specifically on those areas, rather than the whole body, prevents nearly all of the matting this breed experiences.

faq.q: How does field or hunting work change the grooming routine?
faq.a: An Irish Setter that hunts or hikes regularly needs a debris check after every outing, not just a weekly brush. Burrs, seed heads, and mud worked into the feathering during a run through cover will felt into mats within days if left alone, and grass awns can migrate under the skin or into the ears if not removed promptly. Owners of working or heavily exercised Setters should treat the post-outing check as part of the routine, not an occasional extra.
